newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW - ERA eyes more uranium sales.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW - ERA eyes more uranium sales.

text.p: Energy Resources of Australia Ltd is studying options for increasing sales of uranium to France following endorsement by Paris of a ban on tests of nuclear weapons, ERA managing director Phil Shirvington said on Friday.

Shirvington welcomed France's inclusion in the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty this week, saying it would clear the way for the Australian government to lift its restrictions on exports of uranium to the lucrative French market.
Shirvington said ERA had the capacity to more than triple its sales to France, estimated at 300 tonnes last year.
Signing of the ban helped boost ERA shares 25 cents to A$6.25 on Friday, the highest close since June 1995.
"We could increase sales under existing contracts or we could extend the existing contract which expires in 2001," Shirvington told Reuters in an interview.
The market for uranium should be strong for the next three or four years before leveling off, providing a window for growth, Shirvington said.
Uranium currently fetches about US$16.00 a pound, up from less than $12.00 last year on the spot market.
Analysts believe prices have further to go on the upside despite more supply coming on stream.
"There is room for all the major new contracts that are on the drawing board now without crowding out the market," Shirvington said.

ERA produced about 3,500 tonnes of uranium oxide at its Ranger operation in the Northern Territory last year but expects to lift output to 5,000 tonnes by next July when the Orebody Three deposit is developed, Shirvington said.
Rival WMC Ltd also hopes to raise uranium output from its Olympic Dam mine in South Australia to around 3,700 tonnes from 1,500 currently.
RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd also is readying its Kintyre deposit in Western Australia for development.
Production would start about two years from final approval.
Market prices should continue to improve as nuclear power gains wider acceptance, Shirvington said.
"We're expecting prices to plateau off around 1999 or 2000," he said.
"But the next few years is very good time to be writing new long-term business, which would extend out for the next 10 to 15 years," he said.

At present, in Australia only ERA is permitted to export uranium to France, although government constraints imposed in protest of French nuclear bomb tests in the South Pacific, limit shipments to a small fraction of the country's requirements.
Asia and the U.S. represent the largest markets for ERA, but France is also an important destination, Shirvington said.
France has emerged as one of the world's biggest markets for uranium after the country embraced nuclear power generation following the oil shocks of the 1970s.
Electricite de France, the national power company, is the world's single largest buyer of uranium, Shirvington said.
ERA is 68.4 percent-owned by Australian mining company North Ltd.
